For Prompt A, mark each: S speciﬁc · V vague · X invented.
1. For example, many people like it.
2. For instance, a nurse who works night shifts can order groceries at two in the morning and have them
delivered before she wakes up.
3. Research shows that 87% of people prefer online shopping.
4. When a large online seller becomes popular in a town, small bookshops and electronics shops are often the
ﬁrst to close, because they cannot match its prices.
5. There are many examples of this in my country and other countries.
6. A trip to a shopping centre can take two hours including travel, while an online order takes a few minutes.

11

examples
without
meaning
(Prompt
A)
1. The two examples have no detail that shows convenience (no time, eﬀort or place). (2) There is no
Interpretation: it never says what the examples prove. (3) The last sentence adds a new vague fact instead
of linking back to the question.
Fixed
(7-style): "Online shopping saves busy people a great deal of time. A parent who works full time, for
example, can order the week's groceries in ten minutes after the children are asleep, instead of spending
Saturday morning in a crowded supermarket. This shows that buying online gives back hours that working
families have very little of."
Disadvantage
paragraph
·
Band
6-style
One disadvantage of online shopping is that local shops are closing. For example, many shops in my city have
closed in recent years. People prefer to buy things on the internet because it is cheaper and easier. This is a big
problem for the city and the shop owners.
Why
6-style: a clear claim, but the evidence is vague ("many shops") and the last sentence states a problem
without explaining it.

Disadvantage
paragraph
·
Band
7-style
The main drawback of buying online is the damage it does to local shopping streets. When residents order
books, clothes and electronics from large websites, the small shops that sell these goods lose the regular
customers who kept them open, and many close within a few years. This shows that the convenience of one
click has a hidden cost: the street becomes a row of empty windows, and the jobs and daily contact it provided
disappear with it.
Why
7-style: speciﬁc pattern, a cause, and an Interpretation that says what the evidence proves.
Disadvantage
paragraph
·
Band
8-style
The most serious cost of this shift falls on town centres rather than on shoppers. Independent retailers depend
on a steady ﬂow of passing customers; once a large share of everyday purchases moves online, that ﬂow thins,
rents become harder to cover, and the most specialised shops, such as bookshops and repair stores, tend to
close ﬁrst. In other words, each individually sensible choice to order from home adds up to a collective loss:
fewer local jobs, fewer reasons to visit the centre, and a street that no longer works as a meeting place.
Why
8-style: a precise claim, a cause-and-eﬀect chain, careful language ("tend to"), and an Interpretation that
explains the wider consequence.
Step
14
key
·
Band
7-style
Online shopping gives people in small towns the same choice as people in big cities. A student in a rural area
who needs a particular science textbook, for instance, can now order it in minutes instead of travelling to the
capital. This shows that the internet removes a disadvantage that small-town residents once simply had to
accept.
